title: Kestrel and the Well
premise: Xanthe Vasquez, a property surveyor with a habit of counting things to stay sane, is sent to appraise Hollowmere House, a derelict estate whose appraisal figures keep rewriting themselves. The house's mirrors lag one second behind reality, and in that stolen second Xanthe glimpses the previous owners — a choir who drowned a girl in the well and were made to sing her back. As the frost creeps inward from the glass, Xanthe must learn the song's final verse from the drowned girl's ghost without singing along, because the verse only frees her if one living voice stays silent. In the end, Xanthe holds the silence while the house's trapped chorus finishes the song, shattering the mirrors and collapsing the well — but the last appraisal comes back listing Xanthe as the property, a debt the house intends to collect.
about_author: Tamsin Dravenmoor is the pen name of a former land registry clerk from the Norfolk fens who spent years cataloguing houses no one would buy twice. She writes horror about buildings that remember, and refuses to own mirrors.

chapters.title: The Figures Don't Add
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Arriving at Hollowmere House on a grey November morning, Xanthe begins the survey and notices the square footage recalculates itself in the margins of their notes. The emotional beat is professional unease curdling into superstition; the house is already watching the watcher.

chapters.title: Twenty-Two Doors
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. The floor plan shows twenty-one doors; Xanthe counts twenty-two, and the extra one is always behind them. They keep the lights on and start a ritual of counting doors aloud each morning. The beat is the first bargain with compulsion — counting as armor.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. In the hallway mirror, Xanthe's reflection raises its hand a beat after they do. They test every mirror in the house; each lags by exactly one second. The beat is vertigo — the self becoming an unreliable witness in one's own story.

chapters.title: The Room in the Middle
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. The lagging reflections show a room Xanthe has never entered: a parlor with a wellhead in its floor. When Xanthe turns to find the parlor, the corridor geometry refuses. The beat is claustrophobia — the house has a center it will not surrender.

chapters.title: Previous Owners
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV, with archival documents. In the county records office Xanthe finds the 1961 choir of Hollowmere — seven names, six death certificates, one girl, Edith Marlow, listed as 'removed.' The beat is the horror of paperwork: the crime is filed, stamped, and ignored.

chapters.title: Frost on the Inside
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Overnight, frost ferns bloom on the interior of every window, forming spiral patterns that match the wellhead's ironwork. The temperature inside begins dropping faster than outside. The beat is the clock starting — winter is not weather here, it's a deadline.

chapters.title: What the Mirror Keeps
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. The lag stretches to two seconds, and in the gap Xanthe sees the choir standing behind them, mouths open, singing nothing. Their reflection has begun mouthing words they don't know yet. The beat is dread of one's own face becoming a stranger's instrument.

chapters.title: Edith
chapters.summary: Edith's POV, the first intrusion. From inside the well, Edith Marlow remembers the choir's hands, the cold water, and the promise they made her: they would sing her back up. The beat is grief with a blade in it — she is not a haunting, she is an unpaid debt.

chapters.title: The Song Without a Last Verse
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. The choir's melody seeps through the walls at night; Xanthe transcribes it and finds it ends mid-phrase, a song amputated. Singing even a bar of it makes the frost jump a foot across the floor. The beat is temptation — the song wants a mouth.

chapters.title: The Appraisal That Appraises Back
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Xanthe submits a preliminary valuation; the returned document lists the house's value as 'one voice, held.' The bank's stamp is genuine. The beat is institutional horror — the system itself is a limb of the house.

chapters.title: Doors That Were Never Counted
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. The twenty-second door finally opens onto the parlor with the wellhead, and inside, the choir waits in their 1961 clothes, patient as furniture. Xanthe flees, but the corridor now leads back to the parlor from every direction. The beat is the trap closing — the center has found them.

chapters.title: Loyalty of the Living
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Xanthe's sister Priya arrives, worried after weeks of silence, and Xanthe lies to her — badly — to keep her out of the house. Priya sees through it and stays anyway. The beat is love against duty: Xanthe's instinct to protect by exclusion fails against someone who refuses to leave.

chapters.title: What Edith Was Owed
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. Edith shows Priya, through frost patterns on a window, the whole night of 1961: the choir's fear, their crime, and the bargain the house offered them — sing forever, and the well stays shut. The beat is justice outside the law; the law filed her away, the house kept her, and only truth can settle it.

chapters.title: The Verse in the Frost
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. The frost on the windows begins spelling notation — the missing last verse, one line per night, as the cold deepens. Priya copies it down and realizes the final line requires a voice that stays silent while the rest sing. The beat is terrible comprehension: silence is not absence, it's the price.

chapters.title: Counting Fails
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Xanthe's counting ritual breaks — the doors now number twenty-three, then twenty, and the numbers lie fluently. Stripped of their armor, Xanthe panics and nearly sings along to stop the noise in their skull. The beat is the collapse of coping mechanisms under supernatural pressure.

chapters.title: The Choir's Confession
chapters.summary: Xanthe and Priya's alternating POV. The choir, in the parlor, finally speaks: they drowned Edith to save their own children from the well, and the house has held them singing ever since. They ask Xanthe not for forgiveness but for a verdict. The beat is moral vertigo — monsters with reasons, victims with teeth.

chapters.title: Justice Outside the Law
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Xanthe drafts a new appraisal — not of the house but of the crime — assigning value and debt in the only language the house respects: figures, signatures, terms. The house accepts the document as binding. The beat is grim ingenuity — using bureaucracy as a weapon against the thing that owns bureaucracy.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. In the wellhead's dark, Edith teaches Xanthe the final verse note by note, and warns them: when the choir reaches it, the silence will feel like drowning, and the song will beg for Xanthe's voice specifically. The beat is intimacy across death — trust given to a stranger with a counting habit.

chapters.title: Frost Writes Its Final Pattern
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. The frost completes its spiral across every window and mirror at once; the house seals itself, the doors vanish, and the choir begins to sing in the parlor. The beat is the point of no return — the deadline arrived, and the only exits are the ones the song provides.

chapters.title: One Voice Held
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV, climax. The choir sings the last verse while Xanthe holds absolute silence against the song's pleading, the well rising through the parlor floor toward their open mouth. Priya anchors them, counting aloud for them. Edith rises with the water, and the verse completes. The beat is sacrifice through restraint — the hardest thing Xanthe does is nothing.

chapters.title: The Well Closes
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Every mirror shatters inward, the well collapses to dry stone, and the choir — six voices and Edith's — fades mid-harmony, released. The house goes quiet, ordinary, and cold in the way normal houses are. The beat is exhausted, disbelieving relief; the debt is paid, the song is sung.

chapters.title: Appraised
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV, resolution with a hook. Back home, Xanthe receives the final valuation: the property listed is Xanthe Vasquez, appraised at 'one voice, held, pending collection,' signed by a hand that writes in frost. Xanthe covers every mirror in their flat and begins counting doors. The beat is survival with a shadow — the house lost the verse, but it keeps the paperwork.
